legacy_report:
SOURCE: "UQ: Assessing Language Models on Unsolved Questions", Fan Nie*, Ken Ziyu Liu* (co-leads), Zihao Wang, Rui Sun, Wei Liu, Weijia Shi (U Washington), Huaxiu Yao (UNC), Linjun Zhang (Rutgers), Andrew Y. Ng, James Zou, Sanmi Koyejo, Yejin Choi, Percy Liang, Niklas Muennighoff* (Stanford; Muennighoff also Contextual AI). arXiv:2508.17580v1 [cs.CL], 25 Aug 2025. Preprint, no venue stated. Platform: uq.stanford.edu. Funded by Laude Institute.

COVERAGE: 197,256 of 197,256 chars of the cleaned extraction (the raw extraction was 217,917 chars; I removed a repeated logo-footer string from each "UQ" mention). Read in full: abstract, intro, sections 2-8, appendices A, B, C, D (opening), and the Table S2-S8 results. Skimmed only: reference list, and Appendix E (E.1-E.7: sample questions, sample judgment traces, sample verified answers, prompts), about 90k chars of sample text and prompts. I read the E headings and C.3 but not the sample bodies. Page numbers were not recoverable from the extraction, so "where" gives section or table.

TARGET NOTE: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/notes/03-eval-datasets.md (50,784 chars).
Best-fit section: "Lessons from public benchmarks". Its HLE bullet, the adversarial-filtering bullet, is the nearest neighbour. A second home is "Where tasks come from" (a table row for a community source with engagement signals). A third is "Splits, versioning, contamination" (the version-trigger and semi-live dataset rules).
The note already covers:
- HLE filtering against frontier models, with the warning about near-zero scores.
- Filter-model bias (SWAG, HellaSwag, PIQA, BrowseComp).
- Row rejection budgets (SWE-bench Verified, BrowseComp, OSWorld).
- Versioning and review dates (FreshQA).
- Human-baseline audits and expert-grading agreement (GHOSTS).
It has no mention of UQ, Nie or unsolved questions.
It lacks:
- the "no ground truth" paradigm
- an engagement-signal funnel for sourcing hard real rows
- oracle-free validators, and their precision/recall numbers
- validator self-bias and ranking instability when there is no gold
- a rule for retiring solved rows

CORE CLAIM: A benchmark can be both difficult and realistic if it uses real questions that remain unanswered after a long time. These have no gold answers, so a validator pre-screens candidate answers and humans verify the survivors. The paper itself says the validators are often wrong and cannot produce a leaderboard on their own.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Funnel from raw pool to dataset: 3M+ unanswered Stack Exchange questions from 80 sites go to 500.
  number: 33,916 (1.13%) after rules; 7,685 (0.26%) after LLM filter; 500 (0.02%) final; 25-question diamond subset; 30-question dev set with ground truth
  setup: Stack Exchange crawl; the final stage is human review by PhD-level annotators.
  quote: "rule-based filtering trims the pool to 33,916 (1.13% of the original pool), LLM-based filtering prunes to 7,685 (0.26% of the original), and human reviewing ... yields a curated set of 500 items (0.02%)."
  where: Sec 2.2, Table S2
- Rule-filter criteria use engagement as a quality proxy.
  number: age >=2 years; views >=200-2000 and votes >=5-75 (site-dependent); top 10% by votes per site; zero answers
  quote: "Questions must be ≥2 years old." and "Questions must have no answers (as opposed to just having candidate answers not accepted by the original poster)."
  where: Sec 2.1 Stage 1, A.2. A.2 also drops "why" titles, images and tags such as homework or advice.
- LLM filter thresholds (judge o4-mini, 3 calls each; answer model GPT-4o).
  number: binary criteria by unanimous vote; mean answer correctness <=40%; mean expert solvability <=70%
  quote: "have an average of ≤40% answer correctness, and have an average of ≤70% expert solvability to be high-quality and pass them to human review."
  where: Sec 2.1 Stage 2
- The LLM filter makes questions harder by the filter model's own measure (so it inherits filter-model bias).
  number: expert solvability 77.8% to 32.2%; GPT-4o answer correctness 51.2% to 14.1%
  setup: before vs after the LLM filter, judged by o4-mini
  quote: "the averaged expert solvability dropped from 77.8% to 32.2% ... and answer correctness by GPT-4o as the answer model drops from 51.2% to 14.1%"
  where: Sec 2.2, Fig 3
- Generator-validator gap: validating is easier than answering on hard questions.
  number: o3 answers 20% of HLE correctly but validates at 65%
  setup: 500 non-multiple-choice HLE text questions; the same validators transfer to the 30-question UQ dev set without tuning
  quote: "even though the strongest model has poor answer accuracy (e.g., o3 at 20%), it achieves a non-trivial validation accuracy of 65%."
  where: Sec 3.1, Fig 5a/5b. Fig S1 (5 models) is noisier.
- Precision stays low even for the best validator, and stricter voting trades recall for precision.
  number: Best UQ-Validator (2-model 3-Iter unanimous): accuracy 85.40, precision 40.00, recall 24.62. Single-model o3 3-Iter: 81.65 / 30.99 / 34.38. 5-Iter o3: 81.50 / 26.23 / 25.40. o3 vanilla prompt: 58.12 / 20.73 / 78.46.
  setup: 500 HLE question-answer pairs (100 per answer model, 5 models), ground truth withheld from the validator; precision measured against HLE gold
  quote: "the best performingUQ-Validator still has limited precision at 40% (high false positives)" and "the 5-iter o3 validator lowers both precision and recall relative to the 3-iter version"
  where: Sec 3.3 Finding #2, Table 1, Table S7. The base rate of correct answers is low, which caps precision.
- LLM validators over-rate themselves and sibling models.
  number: none
  quote: "we observe similar bias by all frontier models in the form of over-optimism for evaluating self and sibling models (those from the same model developer)"
  setup: HLE surrogate; Gemini favors itself, Claude over-rates all models, o-series over-rate o-series. The o3 3-Iter pipeline largely removes the bias (Finding #4). Bias shrinks from o3-mini to o3 but is not eliminated.
  where: Sec 3.3 Finding #3/#4, Fig 7
- Model rankings flip across validators of different strength.
  number: none
  quote: "every answer model (Gemini, o3, o4-mini, o3-mini) occupies first place under at least one validator"
  setup: 6 validators, 5 answer models on HLE; ranking converges to ground truth only at the strongest validator
  where: Finding #5, Fig 8. Authors' conclusion: oracle-free validators alone should not build leaderboards.
- A better generator is not necessarily a better validator.
  number: none
  quote: "without any pipeline validation, o3 is a weaker answer model yet a stronger validator compared to Gemini 2.5 Pro."
  where: Finding #6, Fig 9
- Human agreement check is tiny.
  number: 25 questions (20 math, 5 non-STEM); Gemini 2.5 Pro: validator pass 12%, human pass 4%, agreement 92%, Cohen's kappa 0.468. Kappa is undefined for the other three models because everything was judged wrong.
  quote: "For Gemini 2.5 Pro as the answer model which produced (only) one correct answer, the coefficient is 0.468"
  where: Table 2, Table S6
- Model results on the 500 questions are very low.
  number: validator pass: o3-pro 75/500 (15.0%), o3 44/500 (8.8%), Gemini 2.5 Pro 25/500 (5.0%), o4-mini 25 (5.0%), DeepSeek-R1 11 (2.2%), Claude Opus 4 7 (1.4%), Claude Sonnet 3.7 6 (1.2%), GPT-4o 0. Unique questions passed 144/500 (28.8%). Human-verified correct: 10 of the 91 verified (of 144). o3-pro 4/46. Diamond subset: 4 passed the validator, 0 of 3 human-verified were correct.
  setup: o3 3-Iter pipeline as validator; human checks partial (limited expert availability), dated 2025-08-26
  quote: "A total of 10 questions passed our secondary human validation" and "The selection of human-rated answers is biased toward wrong answers, as it is easier to prove an answer wrong than correct."
  where: Sec 5, Table 3
- Failure the validator missed: fabricated references.
  quote: "A common failure mode is the model citing references that do not exist, which our UQ-Validator failed to catch"
  where: Sec 5, Sec 7.2
- Versioning rule for a semi-live set.
  number: new version considered when at least 20% of the dataset is verified solved
  quote: "A potential criterion for issuing a new dataset version is when at least 20% of the UQ-Dataset is considered solved, as manually verified by qualified domain experts."
  where: A.5. Sec 2.3: solved questions may be removed and replaced. App. C.3 adds a human baseline of 2/500, and those questions were kept for version consistency.
- Composition is STEM-heavy, with a few sites supplying most rows.
  number: MathOverflow 200, Mathematics 108, TCS 41, Stack Overflow 21, SF&F 35; Science 395 of 500 (78.8%)
  quote: "We do not claim that theUQ-Dataset is broadly representative of unsolved questions in the wild"
  where: Table S3/S5, Sec 7.1. For many sites the human stage simply took top-k by votes (e.g. MathOverflow top 200).
- Test-time scaling and ensembling of validators, with diminishing returns.
  number: none; more calls help, 2-model unanimous is best
  where: B.5 Finding #7, Fig S2.

LIMITS
Stated by the authors:
- Questions may be unsolved from lack of attention, not intrinsic difficulty.
- Human-review budget is modest.
- Source is Stack Exchange only, with a STEM skew.
- Validator evaluation uses a surrogate (HLE) that may not match UQ's distribution.
- Cost and latency kept some systems untested (Grok 4, o3-deep-research).
- Validators miss hallucinated citations.
- Early platform users are LLM hobbyists.
- Sparse signal: models solve almost nothing, so there is little ranking power.
- Platform needs moderation against abuse.
- Verification is partial, and human-checked answers lean toward wrong ones.
Not stated, my reading:
- Difficulty is defined partly by the same models being tested (GPT-4o answers, o4-mini judges, and o3/Gemini/Claude answers shown to reviewers). This is the filter-model bias the note already describes.
- The validator precision numbers come from HLE, where about 13-16% of answers are correct. The paper does not report UQ precision.
- No intervals anywhere. Table 3 has a human verification denominator of 91 of 144, with tiny per-model counts.
- Validators are run at temperature 0.0 and the numbers rest on one run.
- The 25-item agreement check is not a measure of validator accuracy on UQ.
- Dated: model set is mid-2025 (o3, Claude 3.7, Gemini 2.5). Results will move as questions get solved.

BUILDS ON (as printed): Humanity's Last Exam [41] (surrogate dataset and benchmark design); GPQA [43] (diamond subset idea); Stack Exchange API [46]; self-evaluation bias work [38, 55, 62, 59, 10] (including Goel et al. 2025, "Great models think alike"); MT-bench/Chatbot Arena judge work [66], [3]; the test-time-scaling references [24, 20]; chain-of-verification (Dhuliawala et al. 2023); Prometheus, FLASK, PandaLM, AlpacaFarm for judge methods; benchmark-manipulation work [15, 45]; measurement-validity critiques [48, 44]; Lean [32] for domain validators.

CODE: none. The prompts are in Appendix E.6 and E.7, which I did not read in full.

FIGURES (not extracted with the figures script; captions taken from the text):
- Fig 2 (Sec 2): dataset creation funnel (3M to 33,916 to 7,685 to 500, 25 diamond). Best candidate for the note: one picture of a sourcing pipeline with counts per stage.
- Fig 5a/5b: the generator-validator gap, and transfer to the dev set.
- Fig 6: default validator pipeline (cycle consistency, then fact/logic check, then correctness, each x3 iterated reflection with unanimous vote).
- Fig 7: self and sibling bias heatmap.
- Fig 8: rank instability across validators.
- Table 1 and Table 3: the precision/recall and pass-rate tables.
